Habitat requirements: mature broadleaf woodland, esp oak. with well grown canopy (uncrowded), humidity, standing dead wood. The declines appear to be linked to chicks not surviving to adulthood, specifically chicks not having enough food.

Mainly develops in the small bracket fungus Inonotus radiatus which grows especially on the dead trunks of alder Alnus, also willow Salix & birch Betula; adult once reported from under beech Fagus bark in winter. Most records are from ancient woodlands and wood pastures. Also found on I. dryadeus fruiting on oak Quercus in Co Fermanagh and Phellinus pini in Aberdeenshire.

Develops in decaying branchwood; most often associated with hornbeam Carpinus, oak Quercus, and beech Fagus, but also horse chestnut Aesculus. Generally found on lower dead branches which have been shaded out by the tree's own canopy. Scattered across lowland southern Britain, into the Welsh Marches, but not known from the southwest. Mainly in ancient wood pastures, but occasionally in ancient woods.
Formerly confined to Scottish Highlands, but now also in East Anglia. Has been found in association with oak Quercus in Suffolk, as well as pine Pinus.

Larvae probably develop in decaying heartwood (including red rot) of assorted broadleaved trees e.g oak, lime, plane and willow. Found in woodland, pasture-woodland, hedged farmland and sometimes gardens and other urban situations. Visits hawthorn and willow flowers in spring.

Develops in decayed heartwood of birch Betula, beech Fagus, hawthorn Crataegus and probably other trees; pupate at end of season and hibernate as adult; adults attracted to hawthorn blossom. Primarily associated with ancient wood pastures. Concentrated in Hants and E.Midlands.

often associated with dead ivy and hawthorn, they have been recorded from a wide range of deciduous trees including ash, beech, chestnut, lime, oak, hazel, birch, box and sycamore, on the continent also from pine and we have found them beneath areas of dead bark on an otherwise healthy yew tree in a Watford wood. On dead branches, twigs or in litter.
Tree species: ivy, hawthorn, ash, beech, chestnut, lime, oak, hazel, birch, box, sycamore, yew

Habitat requirements: in moss growing on the base of tree-trunks or on rotten stumps
Adults and larvae under fungoid bark on sound timber of various broad-leaved trees, where moist interface; also in fungi growing on wood; general scavengers, feeding on insect material;
In nests and runs of jet ant Lasius fuliginosus in woodland.
Larvae probably predatory in borings of anobiid beetles; adults usually found by sweeping beneath trees or at umbel flowers.
At slime moulds under fungoid bark, pine Pinus and birch Betula; a northern species best known from Caledonian pine forests, but also recently in SW Yorkshire.
damp and shaded woodland with plenty of decaying timber but the species is also likely to occur on isolated trees in hedgerows or even domestic gardens
Associated with rotten wood, various broad-leaved trees, in woodland; widespread in Britain, although local.

According to Chandler (2018) the biology is unknown with a suspected link to bracket fungus (Phellinus pomaceus) which is associated to old fruit trees (Rosaceae. Spp), thus links to old orchards. On a wider scale preservation of these could benefit the species although the population is either small or under recorded.
Develops in fruiting bodies of Inonotus radiatus on decaying alder trunks.
resource: bracket fungus Mensularia radiata / Inonotus radiatus

Habitat requirements: Larvae form galls under brackets of Ganoderma applanatum; . Presumed to be a recent establishment as the galls are conspicuous and records increasing.

Develops in decaying branchwood of oak Quercus, and to a lesser extent other broad-leaved trees. Branches still attached to tree. Alexader, 2002: found on lower dead branches which have been shaded out by the tree's own canopy. Gielen et al 2022 reports thin dead branches. Associated with fungi.

Larvae in dying boughs of Salix caprea and S .cinerea, especially recently split poles; also reported in oak Quercus. Very restricted distribution in south-east, with old record from Wyre Forest. Possibly associated mainly with old wood pasture commons.
Mature deciduous woodland. Larvae feed on lichens such as Usnea barbata
